evidence: Abstract & Sec.3 (pp.1,4-8): SHAP/LIME stability on 4 tabular credit datasets is the stated aim
read_from: Accepted manuscript arXiv:2509.01409 (states published in EJOR, doi 10.1016/j.ejor.2025.05.039)
problem: Whether instance-dependent cost-sensitive (IDCS) loss functions change the stability of SHAP and LIME explanations in credit scoring.
method: Traditional vs IDCS variants of XGBoost, logistic regression, random forest and neural network (8 models). Training sets resampled to default rates of 1-30% with 25 resampling iterations per rate; SHAP and LIME feature-importance rankings recomputed on the test set each iteration.
data: Four public credit datasets: GMSC (112,915 x 10; 6.74% default), VUB (18,667 x 20; 16.95%), HMEQ (5,960 x 12; 19.95%), South German Credit (1,000 x 20; 30%) (Table 2, p.5).
evaluation: Performance: AUC, AP, Brier, savings, relAEC (new). Stability: coefficient of variation (attribution values) and Sequential Rank Agreement (rankings). Friedman test with Hommel-adjusted post-hoc tests for performance (pp.13-14). Baseline: cost-insensitive counterpart of each model.
findings: IDCS classifiers improve cost-efficiency but yield significantly less stable SHAP and LIME explanations than traditional models; stability falls as class imbalance rises for all four model types, more strongly for IDCS models (abstract; Sec.6).
limitations: Authors: future work on cost distributions, synthetic data, alternative cost matrices and more stable XAI (Sec.6). Ours: instability is induced by retraining on resampled data, so explainer sampling noise (LIME) is not separated from model variation; no input-perturbation or prediction-preservation analysis.
repro: Public datasets; supplementary material cited; no code link found in the full text.
qa_notes: Q7 future-work only; Q8 data public, code not linked; Q9 regulatory context (GDPR/AI Act) but no privacy analysis; Q10 25 iterations per rate but seeds and LIME randomness not separated.

evidence: Abstract, Secs.4-6 (pp.1,6-15): LIME stability indices on tabular credit-risk data
read_from: Preprint arXiv:2001.11757 (compiled 13 Nov 2020) of the JORS article
problem: LIME gives different explanations for the same instance across repeated calls; the paper proposes indices to detect this instability.
method: Derives the sampling distribution of LIME's weighted ridge coefficients and proposes two indices: Variables Stability Index (concordance of selected features) and Coefficients Stability Index (equality tests on coefficients) across repeated LIME calls.
data: Credit-scoring data from CRIF S.p.A.; 56,311 observations (39,418 training and 16,893 test), about 100 initial variables with top 20 retained (Sec.6 dataset-composition table).
evaluation: VSI and CSI (0-100) over 10 repeated LIME calls using the 7 most important features; logistic regression benchmark vs gradient boosting trees; kernel width and ridge penalty varied (pp.14-15). No external baseline stability metric.
findings: Stability depends strongly on LIME hyperparameters: for the same applicant VSI 89.44% / CSI 92.7% (kernel width 3, ridge 1) versus VSI 14.17% / CSI 57.46% (kernel width 1.3, ridge 0.001) (p.15). High dimensionality erodes LIME locality.
limitations: Authors: indices guarantee concordance, not fidelity; framework relies on a ridge local model (Sec.7). Ours: single proprietary dataset, illustrative instances, no input perturbation.
repro: Code: github.com/giorgiovisani/LIME_stability (p.2); data proprietary.
qa_notes: dataset size is reported (56,311), so this score corrected from source evidence; Q4 no competing stability measure; Q6 case-study evidence; Q8 code yes, data no; Q9 regulation discussed; Q10 repeated calls isolate sampling noise.; Q3: Section 6 reports 56,311 observations, train/test counts and the retained predictors.; Q7=0.5: original appraisal retained; supporting extracted limitations: Authors: indices guarantee concordance, not fidelity; framework relies on a ridge local model (Sec.7). Ours: single proprietary dataset, illustrative instances, no input perturbation.

evidence: Abstract, Secs.4-5 (pp.1,4-6): LIME stability method evaluated on tabular breast-cancer and simulated data
read_from: arXiv:2106.07875 version of the KDD'21 paper (doi 10.1145/3447548.3467274)
problem: Random generation of perturbation samples makes LIME explanations unstable across runs.
method: S-LIME: hypothesis tests based on a central limit theorem for LARS/LASSO variable-entry decisions decide adaptively how many perturbation samples LIME needs for a stable top-k feature set.
data: Simulated data; Breast Cancer Wisconsin (569 x 30; random forest, 500 trees, ~95% test accuracy); a sepsis-prediction RNN on temporal EHR data (p.5).
evaluation: Average pairwise Jaccard index of top-k features (k=1..5) over 20 repetitions; baseline: standard LIME with 1,000 perturbations; nmax = 10,000 for S-LIME (Table 1, p.5).
findings: On a breast-cancer test instance, LIME's average Jaccard was 0.61 (k=1), 0.66 (k=4) and 0.59 (k=5), versus 1.0, 1.0 and 0.85 for S-LIME (Table 1).
limitations: Authors: controls sampling variance rather than sensitivity to kernel parameters or model variability; temporal-data explanations remain challenging (Sec.6). Main-text examples focus on selected instances, while Appendix B.2 evaluates 50 test instances per breast-cancer/sepsis application with 20 repeats each. No input-perturbation analysis.
repro: Code: github.com/ZhengzeZhou/slime (p.5); public datasets.
qa_notes: Q6: Appendix B.2 tests50instances per application with20repeats; appraisal retains partial credit because cohort uncertainty intervals are not reported; Q7 scope limits noted; Q8 code and data public; Q9 no personal data beyond public benchmark (N/A); Q10 repetitions control sampling noise.; Q6: Cohort Jaccard averages use 50 instances/application and 20 repeats; uncertainty intervals for the cohort improvement are not reported (Appendix B.2, Table 5).

evidence: Secs.3-4 (pp.2-5): relative stability of 7 explainers on tabular Adult, COMPAS, German Credit
read_from: arXiv:2203.06877 (preprint; presented at an ICLR 2022 workshop)
problem: Existing stability metrics consider only input change and ignore the model's internal representation and output.
method: Proposes Relative Input, Representation and Output Stability (RIS, RRS, ROS) computed over label-preserving perturbations (||x-x'|| <= eps, same predicted class); proves RIS <= lambda * L1 * RRS.
data: Adult, COMPAS, German Credit (tabular); ANN and logistic-regression predictors (Fig.3, App.).
evaluation: RIS/RRS/ROS (log scale) for Gradient, IntegratedGrad, Input*Grad, SmoothGrad, SHAP, LIME and a random baseline; empirical vs theoretical bounds.
findings: No method is completely stable; SmoothGrad is most stable on RRS/ROS, beating others by 12.7% on average; theoretical bounds are on average 233% above empirical values (p.5).
limitations: Authors: none stated beyond motivating limitations of earlier metrics. Ours: short workshop paper, ANN-focused representation metric, no tree ensembles, no statistical testing.
repro: No code link in the paper; public datasets.
qa_notes: Q3 datasets named, sizes not given; Q6 single figure of medians; Q7 no limitations section; Q8 data public, code not linked; Q10 number of perturbations/seeds not detailed.

evidence: Abstract, Sec.3 (pp.1,4-6): stability of TreeSHAP/gain importances of tree ensembles under input and model perturbation
read_from: arXiv:2110.00086 (pre-published version of the CD-MAKE 2021 paper, doi 10.1007/978-3-030-84060-0_19)
problem: Accuracy and stability of global feature-importance methods (gain, TreeSHAP) for tree ensembles had not been compared.
method: Random forest, gradient boosting (sklearn) and XGBoost explained with gain and path-dependent TreeSHAP (global importances). Input perturbation: Gaussian noise with SD of 0.5x, 1x or 2x each feature's SD. Model perturbation: retraining with different seeds/hyperparameters while keeping predictions highly correlated. 50 repetitions (5 for one dataset).
data: Synthetic classification (300 samples, 5-150 features); Forest Fire (517 x 12), Concrete (1,030 x 8), Auto MPG (406 x 7), proprietary Company Finance (2,716 x 892) (Table 1, p.5).
evaluation: Accuracy of top-feature ranking against known synthetic coefficients; stability of importance rankings across perturbed inputs/models; comparison gain vs SHAP across three ensembles.
findings: Global importance methods lack accuracy with and without noisy inputs and become unstable as input dimension or noise increases and when models are re-initialised with different seeds or hyperparameters (abstract, Sec.4).
limitations: Authors: global importances only; one dataset confidential. Ours: local explanations not assessed; mostly regression datasets; statistical tests not reported.
repro: UCI datasets (except proprietary); no code link found in the full text.
qa_notes: Q3 proprietary dataset undisclosed; Q7 limitations brief; Q8 no code link; Q10 50 seeded repetitions.

evidence: Abstract, Secs.2-3 (pp.1-5): SHAP stability vs background-data size on tabular MIMIC-III
read_from: arXiv:2204.11351 (ICLR 2023 Tiny Paper version)
problem: Effect of background-dataset size on the stability of SHAP values and rankings for neural-network models.
method: Three-layer ANN on mortality prediction; background sets of 100-1,000 instances sampled 100 times each; SHAP values and model-level rankings recomputed on the explanation set.
data: MIMIC-III: 44,918 ICU admissions (3,958 positive); 70/30 development/explanation split (p.4).
evaluation: Variance of instance-level SHAP values; quartile-based BLEU and Jaccard (proposed) for ranking stability; no alternative explainer baseline.
findings: SHAP values and rankings fluctuate under small random background sets; fluctuation decreases as background size grows; a U-shape shows top- and bottom-ranked variables are more stable than mid-ranked ones (abstract, Sec.3).
limitations: Authors: single dataset and model family (Tiny Paper scope). Ours: neural model only (not tree ensembles); no input perturbation.
repro: Code publicly accessible (footnote, p.1); MIMIC-III requires credentialed access.
qa_notes: Q4 compares background sizes, no alternative explainer; Q7 brief; Q8 code public; Q9 clinical data, ethics not discussed; Q10 100 resamplings per size.

evidence: Secs.2-3 (pp.2-12): SHAP ranking consistency across 100 seed-varied XGBoost models on Taiwan credit data
read_from: Published article (Risks 2025) via arXiv:2508.01851 PDF
problem: Consistency of SHAP explanations across re-trained probability-of-default models, motivated by adverse-action requirements.
method: 100 XGBoost models with fixed hyperparameters and different random seeds; global SHAP values and ranks compared across models.
data: Default of Credit Card Clients (Taiwan): 30,000 accounts, 23 raw features (79 after one-hot encoding); 22.1% default (pp.2-3).
evaluation: KS statistic, confusion-matrix metrics for performance; Kendall's W for SHAP-rank concordance across 100 models.
findings: KS varied narrowly (41.31-43.63%, median 42.37%), yet SHAP stability depended on importance level: Kendall's W = 0.93 for the top five features vs 0.34 for six mid-importance features (abstract, Sec.3).
limitations: Authors: single dataset, single model class, no hyperparameter tuning (p.13). Ours: global SHAP only; seeds are the only perturbation.
repro: Public dataset; no code link found.
qa_notes: Q4 no comparison explainer or model; Q7 explicit limitations; Q8 data public, code not linked; Q9 regulatory (ECOA/FCRA) framing; Q10 100 seeds.

evidence: Abstract, Secs.3-5 (pp.1-20): SHAP/LIME explanation stability index under business noise on 3 tabular datasets
read_from: Preprint arXiv:2603.05024 (not peer reviewed)
problem: Existing stability measures treat all features equally and lack business meaning; effect of class imbalance (SMOTE) on explanation stability was unexamined.
method: Proposes CIES, a rank-weighted (harmonic) distance between original and perturbed SHAP attributions under a 'business noise' neighbourhood; four tree-based classifiers; raw vs SMOTE-balanced training; LIME re-run to test method-agnosticism.
data: Telco Customer Churn (7,043 x 19), German Credit (1,000 x 20), IBM HR Attrition (1,470 x 31) (p.8).
evaluation: CIES vs uniform (unweighted) baseline using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests over 24 configurations; sensitivity over four noise levels; Lipschitz comparison.
findings: Model complexity affects explanation credibility; SMOTE changes explanation stability as well as performance; CIES discriminates better than the uniform baseline (p<0.01 in all 24 configurations) (abstract).
limitations: Authors discuss weighting choices and a model-smoothness confound (Sec.6). Ours: preprint; prediction preservation not enforced; small datasets.
repro: Public datasets; no code link found.
qa_notes: Q7 robustness checks but limited threats discussion; Q8 no code; Q9 AI Act/GDPR context only; Q10 noise draws described, seeds not reported.

evidence: Abstract, Secs.3,7-9 (pp.1-20): TreeSHAP stability under adversarial perturbation for RF/XGBoost on 4 tabular security datasets
read_from: Preprint arXiv:2607.01679 (not peer reviewed)
problem: Adversarial attacks may destabilise SHAP explanations of tree-ensemble security classifiers even when predictions appear robust.
method: Random forest and XGBoost attacked with five attacks (incl. black-box ZOO, Square Attack, HopSkipJump, plus PGD); TreeSHAP drift summarised in a new Explainability Stability Index (ESI) on the same [0,1] scale as a Robustness Index (RI). Extends an earlier MLP study.
data: Four tabular security datasets: phishing URLs, UNSW-NB15, NF-ToN-IoT, HIKARI-2021.
evaluation: RI (prediction robustness) and ESI (attribution drift) per attack and model; PGD step-size ablation.
findings: ZOO gives degenerate results on XGBoost (RI about 0.98) because of piecewise-constant prediction surfaces, while Square Attack shows real vulnerability (RI about 0.36). Even with near-perfect ZOO robustness, XGBoost ESI is about 0.06-0.16 vs 0.14-0.29 for RF: prediction robustness and explanation stability are distinct axes (abstract).
limitations: Authors discuss attack realism and the PGD anomaly (Sec.10-11). Ours: preprint; adversarial (not random) perturbations; LIME not studied.
repro: Code and results archived on Zenodo (doi 10.5281/zenodo.20968236) (ref.21).
qa_notes: Q7 attack realism discussed; Q8 Zenodo; Q9 no personal data; Q10 repeated runs not clearly reported.

evidence: Secs.2-3 (pp.2-6): SHAP robustness (local Lipschitz) for RF with prediction-preserving neighbourhoods on 4 UCI tabular datasets
read_from: Preprint arXiv:2402.19025 (not peer reviewed)
problem: Random-forest SHAP explanations can change sharply for tiny input changes because a single weak tree switches branch.
method: AXOM: discriminative averaging of weak-learner (tree-level) SHAP explanations to build a more robust ensemble explanation; robustness measured with a local Lipschitz estimate over neighbourhoods where |x_i,a - x_j,a| <= eps and f(x_i) = f(x_j) (eps = 0.01).
data: UCI Wine (13 features), Glass (10), Seeds (7), Banknote Authentication (5) (Table 1, p.5).
evaluation: Local Lipschitz robustness (mean, SD) over 10,000 perturbed points per instance; baselines: decision-tree SHAP and standard random-forest SHAP.
findings: Combining weak-learner explanations improved robustness relative to standard RF SHAP on most datasets; one exception where a decision tree appeared perfectly robust despite lower accuracy (pp.5-6). Shows that crossing a split in one tree makes the Lipschitz ratio diverge.
limitations: Authors: robustness values in arbitrary units, comparison-only. Ours: preprint; tiny datasets; no statistical tests.
repro: Public UCI datasets; no code link found.
qa_notes: Q5 Lipschitz units hard to compare; Q6 small-scale; Q8 no code; Q10 sampling of neighbourhoods described but no repeated seeds.; Q7=0.5: original appraisal retained; supporting extracted limitations: Authors: robustness values in arbitrary units, comparison-only. Ours: preprint; tiny datasets; no statistical tests.

evidence: Abstract, Secs.3-6: multicollinearity-induced SHAP/LIME instability on UNSW-NB15 across four model families
read_from: Preprint arXiv:2605.22529 (not peer reviewed)
problem: Effect of correlated (collinear) features on the stability of post-hoc explanations in intrusion detection.
method: Theorem that multicollinearity inflates attribution variance; dataset-level VIF/correlation audit; linear, tree-based, kernel and neural models on full vs pruned feature sets; Explainability Fragility Score; mitigations CAA-Filtering (grouping attributions) and SHARP (training-time attribution-stability regulariser).
data: UNSW-NB15 network-intrusion benchmark.
evaluation: Kendall's tau across bootstrapped explanations; Explainability Fragility Score; predictive metrics before/after pruning and regularisation.
findings: Explanations and feature importances are non-identifiable under multicollinearity; pruning and SHARP improve explanation stability while predictive performance stays stable (abstract).
limitations: Ours: single dataset; preprint; perturbation is bootstrap resampling rather than input noise.
repro: No code link found in the full text.
qa_notes: Q7 limited threats discussion; Q8 no code/data release beyond public benchmark; Q10 bootstrap repetitions.

evidence: Abstract, Secs.3-5 (pp.1-22): TreeSHAP local stability under prediction-preserving perturbations (LR/DT/RF/XGBoost) on CICIoT2023
read_from: Preprint arXiv:2608.10349 (not peer reviewed)
problem: IDS studies ignore explanation cost and local stability when judging explainable detection.
method: Leakage-safe CICIoT2023 corpus; LR, DT, RF, XGBoost; TreeSHAP cost measured; two perturbation protocols: adversarial and local prediction-preserving (accepted only if predicted class unchanged and confidence change <= 0.05) (p.5); selective-explanation policies.
data: CICIoT2023 (39 features) after deduplication and label-collision removal; natural and balanced test distributions.
evaluation: Top-feature membership, attribution-rank, directional consistency and magnitude drift; TreeSHAP runtime; cost-coverage trade-offs.
findings: At 5,000 samples TreeSHAP took 700.759 s for RF vs 1.471 s for XGBoost; RF showed the strongest base-level stability; XGBoost kept rank and direction but showed more top-feature turnover and magnitude drift (abstract).
limitations: Ours: single dataset; preprint; single explainer.
repro: Code and data archived on Zenodo (doi 10.5281/zenodo.21879038) (p.15).
qa_notes: Q8 Zenodo archive; Q10 prediction-preserving filter and deterministic partitioning.; Q7=0.5: original appraisal retained; supporting extracted limitations: Ours: single dataset; preprint; single explainer.

evidence: Abstract, Results (pp.1,3-11): SHAP stability under post-training quantisation of LR/RF/XGBoost on tabular IEEE-CIS fraud data
read_from: Publisher PDF (Cureus Journal of Computer Science, published 4 Jun 2026; review dates printed)
problem: Whether explanations stay stable when models are compressed by post-training quantisation, given the assumption that preserved accuracy implies preserved explanations.
method: Single FP32 logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost models quantised to INT8 and INT4 without retraining (for XGBoost, quantisation applied at the explanation layer); SHAP explanations compared with the full-precision model.
data: IEEE-CIS Fraud Detection (Kaggle): 420 engineered features; stratified split 354,324 / 118,108 / 118,108 (p.4).
evaluation: Predictive metrics (incl. ROC-AUC); global feature-rank correlation, mean attribution drift and instance-level cosine similarity of SHAP vectors.
findings: Predictive performance and explanation stability were not aligned: nearly identical ROC-AUC was accompanied by noticeable changes in global rankings and local attribution vectors; aggressive (INT4) quantisation caused substantial attribution drift (abstract; p.10).
limitations: Authors: single dataset; XGBoost quantised at explanation layer due to tooling (pp.5,11). Ours: no repeated runs or significance tests.
repro: Data public (Kaggle); no code link.
qa_notes: Q7 explicit limitations; Q8 data only; Q10 single trained model per family, no seeds reported.

evidence: Methods 2.1-2.4, Results (pp.2-13): LIME/SHAP consistency under class imbalance on tabular CPRD EHR data
read_from: Publisher PDF (Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence 8:1682919, 2025)
problem: How class imbalance affects the consistency of LIME, SHAP and PDP explanations for clinical risk models.
method: XGBoost, random forest and MLP trained on several imbalance ratios; explanations compared with a balanced (undersampled) reference model.
data: CPRD UK primary-care records for lung-cancer prediction (anonymised; restricted licence).
evaluation: Jaccard similarity of top-10 features and Rank Agreement vs balanced reference; Mann-Whitney U tests on performance distributions from 100 test-set bootstrap samples (Sec.3.1), and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on explanation-consistency metrics for 100 test instances (Sec.3.2.1).
findings: Explanation consistency degraded as imbalance increased, with differences between LIME and SHAP and across models; balanced training gave more consistent explanations (results).
limitations: Authors: undersampled reference, older CPRD release, no external validation (p.13).
repro: CPRD data restricted; no code link found.
qa_notes: Q8 restricted data, no code; Q9 anonymised data, licence noted; Q10 100 bootstraps.; Q9: Ethics statement reports CPRD ISAC approval, protocol20_014R, and the legally permitted consent waiver; Data availability states restricted CPRD access.

read_from: Publisher PDF (Journal of Computer Science and Technology Studies, published 9 Jan 2026)
problem: Whether explanation stability differs between healthcare-payment and financial-transaction fraud models.

evidence: Abstract, Sec.3 (pp.1,5-6): bootstrap SHAP stability is one of four evaluated components on tabular FICO HELOC (borderline)
read_from: Publisher PDF (Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Review, 2026; peer-review process not stated in PDF)
problem: How to evaluate explainable credit underwriting jointly on profit, fairness, recourse and explanation stability.
method: Logistic regression, random forest (400 trees) and gradient boosting; bad-rate-constrained threshold policies; SHAP explanations; counterfactual recourse; bootstrap (B=5) stability analysis.
data: FICO HELOC (10,459 applicants; 23 bureau features); 70/30 stratified split (p.2).
evaluation: Approval rate, profit, DP/EO fairness gaps, recourse success; stability = Spearman rho of global SHAP and cosine similarity of local SHAP for 50 fixed test instances (Table 3).
findings: Gradient-boosting SHAP explanations were stable (mean Spearman 0.871 global; mean cosine 0.856 local) (abstract).

evidence: RQ2 and Sec.3 (pp.2,9-16): TreeSHAP ranking stability across folds/seeds on tabular engineered features
read_from: Preprint arXiv:2609.28502 (not peer reviewed)
problem: Knowledge-tracing models are opaque; the study tests whether TreeSHAP explanations of a feature-based model are stable and faithful.
method: XGBoost with TreeSHAP on 13 engineered behavioural features vs four deep KT baselines; stability across cross-validation folds, random seeds and two TreeSHAP conditioning schemes; retraining-based faithfulness ablations.

evaluation: AUC; Spearman correlation of global rankings across 15 fold-by-seed runs; ablation of top-ranked features; student-level bootstrap for uncertainty.

evidence: Abstract, Sec.4 (pp.1,6-9): explanation stability of four XAI methods on four UCI tabular datasets vs epistemic uncertainty
read_from: Preprint arXiv:2603.29915 (not peer reviewed)
problem: Explanations are costly and their reliability is not guaranteed; can epistemic uncertainty flag where explanations will be unstable?
method: Five architectures (incl. logistic regression, gradient-boosted trees with an RF surrogate for uncertainty, MLP) and four XAI methods (incl. SHAP and LIME); explanations recomputed under input perturbations (noise and BIM adversarial, epsilon-bounded); stability correlated with epistemic uncertainty; routing and gating use cases.
data: Four UCI tabular classification datasets (Table 1, p.6; 70/15/15 split, z-scored); PlantVillage images as a generalisation check.
evaluation: Spearman's rho and Kendall's tau between original and perturbed attribution rankings; faithfulness measures; correlation with epistemic uncertainty.
findings: Strong negative correlation between epistemic uncertainty and explanation stability across datasets, models and XAI methods; uncertainty also separates faithful from unfaithful explanations (abstract).
limitations: Authors: weak separation when uncertainty has low dispersion; no native uncertainty for LightGBM/CatBoost (pp.10,19).
repro: Code: github.com/comrados/uq-xai (p.1).
qa_notes: Q8 code public; Q10 perturbation types and budgets defined.

evidence: Abstract, Secs.3.6-4 (pp.1,7-14): SHAP ranking stability across seeds and domains for RF/MLP on tabular event data
read_from: Preprint arXiv:2605.10796 (not peer reviewed)
problem: Whether interpretations of football-performance models remain stable when transferred from elite to university football.
method: Random forest (TreeExplainer) and MLP (DeepExplainer) trained on elite event data and applied to a university domain; SHAP and a Counterfactual Impact Score; five random seeds (0-4).
data: Top-five European league match event data (WhoScored/Opta; 8:1:1 match-level split) and NTHU university match data (small, private) (pp.5-6).
evaluation: Seed-wise Spearman rank correlation of SHAP importance; cross-domain structural agreement; MAE/RMSE for performance.
findings: Seed-wise SHAP ranking stability was high in elite data (RF 0.932 +/- 0.019; MLP 0.826 +/- 0.050) but low in the university domain (RF 0.420 +/- 0.018; MLP 0.323 +/- 0.178) (p.14).
limitations: Authors: small target-domain dataset (p.6). Ours: regression task outside finance; only five seeds.
repro: Elite data public (WhoScored); NTHU data private; no code link found.

evidence: Secs.2.4, 3.4 (pp.8,16): TreeSHAP rank stability under training-pool resampling for XGBoost/RF on tabular CICIoT2023

problem: Class-imbalance treatments, calibration and explanation stability are rarely examined together in IoT intrusion detection.

read_from: arXiv:2508.09639 version of the Patterns article (doi 10.1016/j.patter.2025.101454)
problem: SHAP values for tree ensembles are reported as point estimates, ignoring their variability.
method: UbiQTree: decomposes SHAP-value uncertainty into aleatoric, epistemic and entanglement components using Dempster-Shafer theory and Dirichlet-process hypothesis sampling over tree ensembles (random forests).

evidence: Abstract, Secs.2-4: stability (run-to-run consistency) of a Shapley estimator on tabular datasets
read_from: Preprint arXiv:2505.08198 ('under review')
problem: Monte Carlo Shapley approximations are slow and their estimates vary between runs.
method: SIM-Shapley: stochastic iterative momentum with adaptive mini-batches, l2 regularisation, negative-sampling detection and bias correction; proofs of linear Q-convergence and variance bounds.
data: Tabular datasets incl. Airbnb, Bank, Bike sharing and (South German) Credit (appendix figures).
evaluation: Consistency (Pearson correlation across repeated runs vs a benchmark), bias vs ground truth, running time; baselines incl. KernelSHAP-type estimators and SAGE.
findings: Reduced computation time by up to 85% while maintaining or improving attribution quality and run-to-run consistency (abstract; eFigs.2-3).
limitations: Authors: online variance estimate uses one mini-batch; higher-order interactions not covered (p.10).

evidence: Abstract, Sec.6 (pp.1,7-8): sampling instability of SHAP/LIME top-K rankings with hypothesis-testing fixes; tabular Adult Census among datasets
read_from: Preprint arXiv:2401.15800v5 (3 Jul 2025); DBLP lists an earlier version titled 'Provably Stable Feature Rankings with SHAP and LIME'
problem: Monte-Carlo sampling makes the top-ranked features from SHAP/LIME unstable across replicates.
method: Retrospective verification of stable ranks via multiple testing, and two sampling algorithms (StableSHAP/SPRT-SHAP, adjusted S-LIME) that identify the top-K set or ranking with bounded family-wise error rate.
data: Tabular benchmarks incl. Adult Census Income; neural-network classifiers (Fig.1, Sec.6).
evaluation: Family-wise error rate of rankings/sets over repeated runs; number of verified stable ranks; compared with Holm-adjusted confidence intervals and plain Shapley sampling/LIME.
findings: Plain Shapley sampling and LIME produced unstable top-5 rankings on Adult; the proposed procedures kept FWER near the nominal alpha (e.g., 0.1) while using computation adaptively (Fig.1; Sec.6).
limitations: Authors: SPRT is conservative; future less conservative designs (p.9). Ours: neural models only; no input perturbation.
repro: Code: github.com/jeremy-goldwasser/feature-rankings (p.2).
qa_notes: Q3 dataset details in appendix; Q7 brief; Q10 repeated replicates with error-rate control.

evidence: Secs.4-5 (pp.5-10): LINEX stability metrics (CI, CAC) on tabular datasets (e.g., IRIS, MEPS) plus images
read_from: arXiv:2201.12143 version of the NeurIPS 2023 paper
problem: LIME and variants give explanations that change across nearby examples and sampling runs.
method: LINEX: local explanations from an invariant-risk-minimisation game over several perturbation environments, eliminating features whose gradient flips sign locally; random and realistic (MAPLE-like) neighbourhoods.
data: Tabular (e.g., IRIS, MEPS and others in Table 3) and image (FMNIST, CIFAR10) datasets; 80/20 splits.
evaluation: Infidelity, generalised infidelity, Coefficient Inconsistency (CI), Class Attribution Consistency (CAC), unidirectionality; baselines LIME, S-LIME, MeLIME, NAS-LIME; paired t-tests (p.9).
findings: LINEX was better than baselines in 21 of 40 cases and worse in 5, with notably better stability metrics (CI, CAC) and unidirectionality (p.9).
limitations: Authors: limitations discussed in Suppl. O (p.11).
repro: No code link found in the full text; public datasets.
qa_notes: Q7 limitations in supplement; Q8 no code link; Q10 multiple environments and reported SDs.

evidence: Abstract and Sec.4 (pp.1,4-5): stability of Shapley-value explanations across a Rashomon set of near-optimal models on tabular data
read_from: Publisher PDF (ESANN 2026 proceedings, pp.145-150)
problem: Near-optimal models (Rashomon set) can give different explanations; consistency of explanations across them is unexplored.
method: Shallow two-layer MLPs trained repeatedly; exact Shapley values (low-dimensional data) and weight-based importance profiles; cluster analysis of importance profiles across the Rashomon set.
data: Pima Indians Diabetes, Wheat Seed, and a third small tabular dataset (Table 1, p.5).
evaluation: Spearman correlation between importance profiles, number of clusters, adjusted Rand index between cluster solutions.
findings: Correlations between importance profiles and agreement of cluster solutions were not very high (e.g., ARI 0.26, 0.092, 0.07), showing qualitatively different explanations among equally accurate models (Table 1).
limitations: Authors: limited to shallow networks (p.4).
repro: No code link found; public datasets.
